meta.description: Not Lord Chesterfield and not Oscar Wilde. An anonymous English newspaper jest from June 1899.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A Gentleman Is a Man Who Never Gives Offense Unintentionally'?
meta.ogDescription: Nobody famous. It began as anonymous newspaper filler in 1899; Chesterfield was credited in 1940.

answer.label: Not Lord Chesterfield — an anonymous newspaper jest from 1899
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented 16 June 1899 · The Bedfordshire Mercury, unsigned
answer.sourceLine: Chesterfield died in 1773, and nobody credited him with this until 1940. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the earliest version in an unsigned humour column, “Pleasant Paragraphs,” in The Bedfordshire Mercury of 16 June 1899: “The well-bred man is never rude unintentionally.” The familiar “gives offence” wording follows in The Saturday Review of London in September 1905, and the American “offense” spelling in January 1906 — all of it anonymous.

source.excerpt: The well-bred man is never rude unintentionally.
trail: Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ is the anchor, and we read it in full. It cites the earliest instance as “1899 June 16, The Bedfordshire Mercury, Pleasant Paragraphs, Quote Page 3, Column 3” (British Newspaper Archive), and tracks reprints in The Widnes Examiner (December 1900) and the St. Helens Examiner (February 1901).

The wording this page is named for is dated from the same chronology: The Saturday Review of London, 2 September 1905, “The best extant definition of a gentleman is ‘a man who never gives offence unintentionally’”; then Clover: A Monthly Magazine of Springfield, Massachusetts, January 1906, page 22, with the American spelling. We were able to confirm that QI’s Clover volume exists and matches its description — Google Books ↗ lists “Clover, a Monthly Magazine, Volume 2; Volume 4,” contributed by Springfield Breweries Co. of Springfield, Mass. — though the page image itself was not visible to us.

The Chesterfield attribution is late and traceable: QI dates it to “1940 November 21, Hawkins Herald, Today and Tomorrow by Frank Parker Stockbridge, Quote Page 3, Column 6,” where a columnist has Chesterfield writing it to his son. Wikipedia ↗ gives Chesterfield’s dates as 1694 to 1773, so the column postdates his death by 167 years. QI calls the attribution “probably spurious.”

Limit of what we checked: the newspaper instances sit in subscription archives (British Newspaper Archive, Newspapers.com, NewspaperArchive) and Google Books returned a bot challenge on every page-image attempt this run. The transcriptions and locators above are Quote Investigator’s, credited to it rather than claimed as our own.

author.name: Anonymous (an English newspaper jest of 1899)
author.heading: About Anonymous (an English newspaper jest of 1899)
author.metaLine: Earliest documented 16 June 1899 · unsigned English newspaper humour · popularly mis-credited to Lord Chesterfield
author.bio: No author is known. The epigram first appears as an unsigned item in “Pleasant Paragraphs,” a miscellany of jokes in The Bedfordshire Mercury of 16 June 1899, and was reprinted in other English papers over the next two years with no attribution. It reached its familiar form in The Saturday Review of London in 1905 and crossed to the United States in 1906, still anonymous. Famous owners were supplied only decades later.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A good anonymous joke attracts famous owners, and this one has collected a statesman, an aesthete and a film star.

items.why: A newspaper columnist in November 1940 presented it as Chesterfield writing to his son. He died in 1773, the joke is first documented in 1899, and Quote Investigator ↗ finds no substantive support for the linkage. The appeal is obvious — Letters to His Son is full of advice on manners — but this is not in it.

Wilde died in 1900, months after the joke first appeared, and the earliest linkage to him that QI located ↗ is a homemaking column by Eleanor Ross on 1 May 1929. QI reports no substantive evidence that Wilde created or used it.

Punch suggested in August 1920 that a compositor had slipped an “un” into a pious definition and invented the joke by accident, and a 1922 anthology repeated the theory. QI’s view ↗ is that the quip was constructed deliberately and the printing-blunder tale was an embellishment of it.

Wayne told an Associated Press interviewer in February 1974: “I try not to unintentionally hurt anybody’s feelings. If I do hurt anybody’s feelings, I had all intention of hurting them.” QI notes ↗ he did make this thematically related statement — it is his, and it is not the epigram.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗: “this joke was being disseminated by 1899, and the earliest instances were anonymous,” and “The linkages to Oscar Wilde and Lord Chesterfield currently have no substantive support.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke is a one-letter edit of Victorian etiquette. The conduct books said a gentleman never gives offence intentionally; add “un” and you get a man whose rudeness is always on purpose — which is both funnier and, as a definition of a certain kind of gentleman, uncomfortably accurate.

That economy is why it keeps getting handed to famous wits. It sounds like something Wilde would have said, so it was given to Wilde; it sounds like worldly advice to a son, so it was given to Chesterfield. Neither needed to exist for the joke to work.
detailsBody: The chronology is unusually well filled in, and it shows a joke circulating on its own merits for thirty years before anyone thought to attach a name. It travels as anonymous filler through English papers from 1899, crosses to American magazines and newspapers by 1906, turns up in an etiquette compendium, a London short story, a Dublin article on manners, and — in 1929 and again in 1933 — as graffiti seen under a film studio desk and on a speakeasy wall.

Only then do the famous names arrive: Wilde in 1929, Chesterfield in 1940. Christopher Hitchens, who had better instincts about this sort of thing, simply called it “an old definition of a gentleman” in 2001 and left it at that.
context.pull: One letter turns a platitude into a character sketch.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator transcribes the earliest instance (“The well-bred man is never rude unintentionally”) from The Bedfordshire Mercury, 16 June 1899, Pleasant Paragraphs, page 3 column 3; dates the “gives offence” wording to The Saturday Review of London, 2 September 1905, and the “offense” spelling to Clover: A Monthly Magazine, January 1906, page 22; dates the Chesterfield credit to the Hawkins Herald of 21 November 1940 and calls it probably spurious; dates the earliest Wilde linkage to Eleanor Ross, 1 May 1929; and concludes the joke was disseminated by 1899 with anonymous earliest instances and no substantive support for Wilde or Chesterfield.
Wikipedia: Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield, 1694–1773, British politician, diplomat and writer.

Google Books lists the volume QI cites as “Clover, a Monthly Magazine, Volume 2; Volume 4”, contributed by Springfield Breweries Co., Springfield, Mass. — matching QI’s bibliographic description. The page image was NOT visible, so the quotation itself was not confirmed here.
